title: Effect of Punching on Residual Stress, Microstructural Changes, and Fatigue Properties of Thick-Plate High-Strength Low-Alloy Steel
abstract: Abstract This work explores the effect of varying punching parameters on the high-cycle fatigue (HCF) response of thick-plate high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel intended for heavy-duty truck chassis. A combination of microstructural characterization, tensile testing, HCF experiments on both punched and unpunched specimens, and neutron diffraction-based residual stress measurements was conducted. The punching operation induces pronounced microstructural modifications, including grain refinement, defect generation, tensile residual stresses, development of a hardened shear-affected zone, and a rough fracture surface inside the punched hole. At higher stress amplitudes and shorter fatigue lives (approximately 10 5  cycles), the HCF behavior after punching remains comparable to that of unpunched specimens and exhibits lower sensitivity to punching-induced changes. In contrast, under lower stress amplitudes and longer lifetimes (around 10 6  cycles), fatigue strength decreases considerably due to the combined influence of surface roughness and, more critically, tensile residual stresses, with fatigue cracks initiating near mid-thickness—the region of highest measured tensile residual stresses. Furthermore, localized deformation during punching promotes microstructural refinement and defect formation, further influencing fatigue resistance. The optimization of punching parameters to balance the hardening benefits with minimal defect and sub-grain formation can improve fatigue performance. These insights offer strategies to enhance fatigue performance of HSLA steel in heavy-duty truck chassis components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels are commonly employed in heavy-duty truck chassis because of their favorable balance between strength and ductility. [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]  Producing these chassis components often involves sheet shearing operations, such as punching or trimming. [ 1 , 4 , 6 , 7 ]  For mass production, mechanical shearing in a press remains more attractive than other cutting techniques due to its high productivity and cost-effectiveness. Consequently, most steel components used in automotive structures are produced using the mechanical blanking process. [ 7 , 8 ]  Punching strongly alters the steel’s microstructure, producing a rough fracture surface inside the punched hole, introducing residual stresses, and forming a shear-affected zone (SAZ) around the hole. The SAZ becomes highly work-hardened and commonly contains defects such as micro-voids and micro-cracks generated during the punching process. These microstructural and stress-related changes reduce the fatigue resistance of steel, leading to a noticeable decrease in post-punching fatigue strength compared to the as-rolled specimens. [ 1 , 2 , 4 , 5 , 9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]  Post-punching effects are strongly influenced by the shear cutting parameters including die clearance, the distance between the punch and the die used during punching, and the geometry of the punch. [ 2 , 9 ]  Several studies have examined how different cutting clearances affect surface roughness, residual stress, and microstructural changes after punching. Increasing the cutting clearance results in more micro-voids, which facilitate failure initiation within the microstructure. [ 13 ,  14 – 15 ]  Shiozaki  et al. [ 4 ]  observed that increasing the cutting clearance led to greater surface roughness and residual stress at the punched edge in two hot-rolled steels. Higher surface roughness around the punched hole is recognized as a major factor contributing to the reduction in the fatigue limit of punched steels, [ 2 , 9 , 10 , 16 ,  17 – 18 ]  as rough surfaces act as initiation sites for fatigue cracks. Similarly, increased tensile residual stresses near potential crack initiation regions adversely affect the steel’s fatigue performance by accelerating crack formation. [ 4 , 18 ]  Gustafsson  et al. [ 19 ]  proposed a model to estimate the reduction in fatigue strength after punching, considering only the effects of surface roughness and residual stress. Applying this model to polished fatigue data, they reported good agreement between experimental and predicted values across various materials, including aluminum and steel. Moreover, Mori  et al. [ 20 , 21 ]  reported that the magnitude of residual stresses after shear blanking varies through the thickness of trimmed specimens, which could affect fatigue crack initiation in punched steels. [ 4 ]  Several attempts have been made to simulate residual stress distribution at sheared edges. [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 ,  25 – 26 ]  These models require validation with experimental data, often obtained by cutting the punched hole and measuring residual stress using focused ion beam techniques [ 26 ]  or laboratory X-ray diffraction, [ 20 , 21 , 27 ]  since measuring residual stress around the punched hole without cutting is experimentally challenging. However, these methods can only measure residual stresses in two directions, and the cutting process may alter the residual stress distribution. Therefore, quantifying residual stress around the hole in punched specimens—particularly in thick-plate configurations—and studying their impact on fatigue performance are essential.

Optimizing the punch geometry is also essential for improving the punching process, as tool life, punching force, and edge quality significantly affect manufacturing efficiency and product performance. Punch geometry directly influences residual stress, surface quality, and dimensional accuracy of punched holes. Flat punches, the most conventional design, engage the material simultaneously, producing the highest punching loads and causing faster tool wear and higher stress concentrations, though they maintain good dimensional accuracy. [ 28 ]  Rooftop punches, particularly those with a 7 deg shear angle, significantly reduce punching loads (by more than 50 pct) by creating a progressive, scissor-like shearing action, although they may introduce slight dimensional inaccuracies like elliptical holes. [ 28 ]  Humped punches help reduce stress concentration and improve edge stretchability by promoting earlier fracture at lower deformation levels, though they have limited effect on reducing overall punching loads. [ 29 ]  Hybrid punches, which combine shear-angled and humped designs, offer a good compromise solution with load reductions of up to 45 pct, enhancing tool life, edge quality, and reducing stress concentration while maintaining reasonable dimensional accuracy. [ 29 , 30 ]

A review of the existing literature on post-punched performance of steels suggests that punching parameters and punch geometry significantly influence key factors affecting post-punching fatigue performance, including surface roughness, microstructural changes, and particularly residual stress. While these factors have been extensively studied in relation to steel edge ductility, there has been little research on how different punching methods influence post-punching fatigue performance. The primary objective of this study is to quantify the residual stress distribution around punched holes and investigate how different punching methods affect surface roughness, residual stress, and microstructural changes in the steel before and after cyclic loading; and correlate these changes with post-punching fatigue performance. Ultimately, this research aims to optimize punching parameters to reduce post-punching fatigue strength degradation in HSLA steels, thereby enhancing the fatigue performance after shearing processes in heavy-duty truck chassis components.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: In this study, a commercial low-carbon hot-rolled HSLA steel (500MC) with a thickness of 8 mm was examined. The chemical composition of the steel is presented in Table  I . Table I Chemical Composition of the Studied Steel (Wt Pct) C Mn Nb Al Ti Fe 0.065 1.35 0.02 to 0.05 0.045 0.03 to 0.06 bal.

Microstructural analysis of the as-rolled specimens was conducted using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) on electrolytically polished samples. A JEOL 7800F scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with a Bruker EBSD detector was employed, operating at 15 kV with a 50-nm step size. Electrolytic polishing was performed at room temperature with 28 V applied voltage in a solution of 10 vol pct perchloric acid and 90 vol pct ethanol prior to EBSD measurement.

Microstructure-unit boundaries were identified using a 2 deg misorientation threshold, which was also employed to calculate the kernel average misorientation (KAM) based on the third nearest neighbors. The EBSD datasets were processed and analyzed using the MTEX open-source toolbox. [ 31 ]

The quasi-static mechanical properties of the studied steel were evaluated using standard tensile tests, in accordance with ISO 6892 guidelines. Three tensile specimens were cut parallel to the rolling direction (RD) and tested in a Galdabini SUN 20 equipment at a displacement rate of 0.01 mm/s. The geometry of the tensile test specimen is shown in Figure  1 (a). Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of ( a ) tensile test specimen, ( b ) smooth unpunched fatigue test specimen, ( c ) punch geometries and corresponding punched fatigue specimen, and ( d ) cross section of a punched specimen. All dimensions are given in mm

HCF tests were performed at a load ratio of  R  =  − 1, with frequencies varying between 2 and 6 Hz at room temperature, using an MTS 810 equipment. After completing the fatigue tests, the fracture surfaces of the punched specimens were investigated using secondary electron (SE) imaging mode with the JEOL 7800 SEM.

The overall morphology of the as-punched cross section was observed using an Olympus BX53M optical microscope. To detect defects generated during the punching process, SE and backscattered electron (BSE) imaging were performed on selected regions within the fracture zone, collected in 100  µ m increments, starting at the punched edge and extending up to 1.5 mm into the longitudinal direction. These areas were further examined using EBSD to evaluate the crystallographic changes caused by punching in the studied steel. All EBSD measurements were conducted with the JEOL 7800F SEM. Before EBSD acquisition, the specimens were mechanically ground and subsequently polished with a colloidal silica suspension to obtain a final surface finish of 0.02  µ m.

To evaluate the width of the shear-affected zone after punching, micro-hardness measurements were carried out within the fracture zone of the punched specimens using a Duramin-40 tester equipped with a Vickers indenter. The tests were performed under a 50 gf load with a dwell time of 10 seconds. The initial two indents were positioned at 30 and 100  µ m from the punched edge, with remaining indents spaced at 100  µ m intervals for the next 13 measurements (Figure  1 (d)).

The surface roughness of all punched specimens was evaluated using interferometric imaging with a Sensofar Metrology S Neox confocal microscope. After fatigue testing, the entire fracture zone of each sample was scanned and mapped, as shown in Figure  1 (d). Based on these surface maps, the average values of different roughness parameters were determined for each punching condition.

To validate the capability of this technique to capture the residual stress gradient in punched specimens, the residual stress variations were measured through the thickness, parallel to the punching direction (ND). For these measurements, a partially immersed GV of 1 × 1 × 2 mm 3  was used, with the GV center positioned at 1 mm (beginning), 4 mm (mid-thickness), and 7 mm (end) from the punch entry point on the sheet surface. Additionally, residual stress variations with distance from the punched edge, parallel to the LD, were also measured. In this case, a fully immersed GV of the same size was used, with the GV center positioned at 1, 2, and 3 mm from the punched edge at mid-thickness of the specimens.

Finally, the exponents  h t  and  h r  vary between 0 and 1, representing the influence of the stress concentration and surface roughness on fatigue life. A detailed explanation of this methodology can be found in Ref [ 19 ].

sections.heading: Post-punching Characteristic
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the cross sections of the as-punched specimens in the longitudinal direction using optical microscopy. Fig. 4 Overview optical micrograph of the as-punched cross section for ( a ) flat, ( b ) RT, ( c ) HB, and ( d ) HBB punches. All the main images and enlarged insets taken by SEM have the same scale bar of 500 and 5  µ m, respectively

The analysis reveals that the HBB punch produces the largest fracture zone compared to the other punching conditions which have nearly similar fracture zone sizes. Additionally, Figures  4 (b) and (c) show that both the RT and HB punches generate large cracks within the fracture zone, highlighted by dashed ellipses, whereas no such cracks are observed in the flat and HBB punches. The RT punch exhibits a higher quantity of these cracks, with some located at the mid-thickness of punched specimen, while in the HB punch, these cracks are formed at the end of the fracture zone. Enlarged BSE images of these cracks in RT and HB punches are shown in Figures  4 (b) and (c), respectively.

To provide a clearer understanding of the influence of punching methods on the formation of micro-defects and the orientation of microstructural units, the punched edge at mid-thickness is examined using SE, and EBSD, as shown in Figure  5 . Fig. 5 EBSD IPF maps with respect to the ND at the punched edge and enlarged SE images of micro-defects near the mid-thickness of ( a ) flat, ( b ) RT, ( c ) HB, and ( d ) HBB punches

The inverse pole figure (IPF)-colored orientation maps with respect to the ND, compared with the as-rolled microstructure in Figure  3 , reveal pronounced microstructural refinement near the punched edge. The RT punch exhibits the most substantial impact on the microstructure, producing the smallest unit size of 1.6  µ m, while the HBB punch has the least effect, with a unit size of 3.9  µ m. The flat and HB punches show nearly similar microstructure unit sizes of 2.8 and 2.5  µ m, respectively. Moreover, the punching process also introduces severe local deformation that promotes the development of micro-defects. Enlarged SE images in Figure  5  confirm that these defects mainly appear at carbide–ferrite interface under all punching conditions.

The residual stress introduced by punching is measured using neutron diffraction (Figure  6 ). Figure  6 (a) illustrates the variation of the residual stress through the thickness of the punched hole made with the flat punch. In the burnish region, the residual stress is around 90 MPa, it increases to a maximum of about 300 MPa at mid-thickness, and then decreases to 50 MPa near the exit side of the punch. Figure  6 (b) shows that at mid-thickness, the residual stress peaks at the punched edge and gradually decreases to a compressive value with increasing distance from the edge, confirming the method's ability to capture the residual stress gradient. Since the maximum residual stress occurs at mid-thickness, measurements for all other punching conditions were also performed at mid-thickness (Figure  6 (c)). The HBB punch exhibits the highest residual stress value of 412 MPa, while the HB, RT, and flat punches show values of 347, 338, and 297 MPa, respectively. Fig. 6 Longitudinal residual stress component variations ( a ) through the thickness for flat punch, ( b ) at mid-thickness and with distance from the punched edge for flat punch, and ( c ) at mid-thickness and near the punched edge for different punching conditions

Figure  7  shows the surface roughness of different punches, the average KAM value, variation in the area fraction of sub-grains—defined as microstructural units with a grain orientation spread (GOS) below 1.5 deg—along with micro-hardness changes at different distances from the punched edge. As shown in Figure  7 (a), the HBB punch has the highest surface roughness ( R z  = 42  µ m), followed by the HB (27  µ m), RT (24  µ m), and flat punches (23  µ m). Figure  7 (b) reveals that average KAM values increase as the distance from the punched edge decreases (see Electronic Supplementary Figure S1). While the average KAM values at the punched edge are nearly identical across all punching conditions, the HBB punch shows lower average KAM values at other distances from the edge. Figure  7 (c) demonstrates that the proportion of sub-grains increases considerably within 0.5 mm of the punched edge. The RT punch exhibits the highest proportion, close to 50 pct, whereas the flat, HB, and HBB punches show values of roughly 35 pct (Figure  7 (c)). Figure  7 (d) shows that the hardness is highest near the punched edge and decreases gradually with distance, reaching a stable level at about 1 mm from the punched edge for all punches, except for the HBB type, which levels off earlier at approximately 500  µ m from the edge. The RT punch has the largest hardness increase (54 pct), followed by the flat (45 pct), HB (40 pct), and HBB (32 pct). Fig. 7 ( a ) Mean surface roughness in the fracture zone, ( b ) changes in average KAM values, ( c ) fraction of sub-grains formed, and ( d ) micro-hardness variation with distance from the punched edge

sections.heading: HCF Performance of Different Punching Conditions
paragraphs: Figure  8 (b) presents a comparison of the experimental post-punching results with  S – N  curves predicted by the model of Gustafsson  et al. , [ 19 ]  which incorporates the effects of residual stresses and surface roughness. While the model predicts that punched specimens exhibit nearly the same fatigue strength at higher stress levels, it fails to capture the significant differences in post-punched fatigue strength among various punching conditions at lower stress levels.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: At around 10 5  cycles, the HCF response of punched specimens is nearly similar to that of the unpunched condition. This indicates that in this regime, fatigue strength was only weakly influenced by variations in surface roughness, tensile residual stress, or microstructural alterations caused by different punching techniques. The reduced sensitivity can be attributed to the loading conditions, where the combination of tensile residual stress and maximum cyclic stress exceeds the yield strength of the steel for all punches, resulting in stress relaxation and reducing the impact of residual stress as a failure initiator.

Such behavior is consistent with earlier investigations showing that, at high-stress amplitudes, local plasticity promotes multiple crack initiation, as observed in Figure  9 , while fatigue failure is largely governed primarily by crack propagation from the most dominant crack rather than by initiation. [ 7 , 16 , 35 ]  Similarly, our earlier work on post-punching fatigue performance demonstrated that fatigue strength at 10 5  cycles is mainly controlled by the fatigue crack growth resistance of steel. [ 36 ]  Consequently, the investigated steel exhibits comparable fatigue strength at higher stresses regardless of the punching method.

As the applied stress decreases, the relative contribution of fatigue crack initiation to the total fatigue life increases. At lower stress levels, near 10 6  cycles, fatigue strength decreases differently among the punching conditions, indicating a transition to an initiation-controlled fatigue regime, where only a single dominant fatigue crack is observed on the fracture surface (Figure  10 ). Unlike the high-stress regime, where multiple initiation sites form rapidly, fatigue life at lower stresses is dominated by the time required to nucleate this dominant crack. Consequently, differences in punching-induced surface condition, residual stress distribution, and microstructural heterogeneity have a greater impact on fatigue strength.

Surface roughness and residual stresses in the fracture zone are regarded as the main factors responsible for the reduction in fatigue strength of punched specimens. [ 2 , 4 , 9 , 10 , 16 , 17 , 19 ]  Surface intrusions and extrusions function as stress concentrators that promote localized plastic deformation, thereby facilitating fatigue crack initiation. [ 2 , 37 ]  In addition, tensile residual stresses in the fracture zone accelerate crack formation, particularly near the fatigue limit, since these stresses are less prone to relaxation during cyclic loading.

A comparison of the surface roughness trends (Figure  7 (a)) and residual stress distributions (Figure  6 (c)) with the  S – N  curves (Figure  8 ) indicates that higher surface roughness and residual stress are associated with reduced post-punching fatigue strength. Among the tested conditions, the HBB punch exhibited the highest levels of both residual stress and surface roughness—likely a consequence of its larger clearance—and consequently showed the most pronounced decrease in fatigue performance. This finding aligns with Reference  4 , where increased residual stress and surface roughness were observed with increasing clearance during punching. Conversely, reducing the clearance in the other punches results in lower measured values of surface roughness and residual stress. Fracture surface analysis at this low applied stress level (Figure  10 ) indicates that fatigue cracks in all punched conditions initiate close to the mid-thickness of the specimens, corresponding to the region of maximum residual stress through the thickness (Figures  6 (a) and (b)). However, the simulated  S – N  curves that account for residual stress and surface roughness (Figure  8 (b)) predict nearly identical fatigue performance for all punches, except for the HBB punch, which has a slightly lower simulated  S – N  curve. This similar estimated reduction, despite significant differences in surface roughness and residual stress—especially for the HBB punch—is likely due to the stress relaxation criteria proposed in Reference  19 . At 10 6  cycles, the same residual stress reduction factor ( K m ) is obtained for all punching conditions, meaning that large experimental variations in residual stress do not translate into proportional differences in simulated fatigue strength. However, the higher surface roughness of the HBB punch contributes to its larger surface roughness reduction factor ( K r ), leading to a higher estimated reduction in fatigue strength for this punch.

Despite this mechanistic explanation, the predictive capability of the model remains limited by its simplified treatment of residual stress relaxation and cyclic plasticity effects. Incorporating more localized cyclic relaxation or plasticity mechanisms could improve prediction accuracy. In addition, accounting for punching-induced microstructural heterogeneity and defect formation within the shear-affected zone may further enhance the model’s ability to differentiate between punching conditions in the initiation-controlled fatigue regime. These findings suggest that residual stress plays a more dominant role than surface roughness in reducing post-punching fatigue strength, emphasizing the importance of quantifying residual stresses when evaluating fatigue performance in punched steels.

A comparison between the as-rolled microstructure (Figure  3 ) and the post-punched microstructures (Figure  5 ) shows pronounced refinement and enhanced work hardening at the punched edge under all investigated punching conditions. Despite nearly identical average KAM values at the punched edge (Figure  7 (b)), indicating similar levels of work hardening, there are significant differences in microstructural unit sizes. This microstructural evolution can be attributed to the rearrangement of dislocations due to localized plastic deformation during punching, consistent with our earlier findings and reports from other studies. [ 38 , 39 ]  In previous work, [ 36 ]  we demonstrated that such refinement delays fatigue crack initiation by increasing local strength, in line with the general trend that higher tensile strength correlates with improved fatigue resistance. [ 40 ,  41 ,  42 ,  43 – 44 ]  This effect is evident when comparing the RT and HB punches. Despite having similar surface roughness and residual stress, the RT punch—with higher hardness near the punched edge (Figure  7 (d))—shows a smaller reduction in fatigue strength, while the HBB punch, with the lowest hardness, records the largest reduction. In contrast, when comparing the flat and RT punches, the flat punch exhibits a smaller reduction in fatigue strength despite its lower hardness at the punched edge. This discrepancy may be linked to punching-induced defects that act as preferential crack initiation sites. [ 1 , 13 , 45 , 46 ]  Examination of cross sections (Figure  4 (b)) and fracture surfaces of fatigued specimens (Figure  10 (b)) support this explanation, showing large cracks near the fatigue crack initiation site in the RT punch. Moreover, the larger fraction of sub-grains (Figure  7 (c)) in the RT punch near the initiation site could facilitate fatigue initiation by lowering the local threshold stress intensity factor range ( ∆K th ), as reported in earlier studies. [ 36 , 47 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 ,  51 – 52 ]  The presence of fatigue cracks within these sub-grains, which appear as dimples on the fracture surface (Figure  10 (b)), could confirm this hypothesis, potentially explaining the lower fatigue strength of the RT punch compared to the flat punch.

These findings suggest that surface roughness and residual stress are the primary factors influencing the post-punching fatigue strength of HSLA steel with a homogeneous microstructure. Therefore, adjusting punching parameters to minimize these effects offers a promising route for improving fatigue resistance after punching. In addition, strain localization and its effects on microstructural refinement and defect formation also play key roles in fatigue properties post-punching. Selecting an appropriate punching geometry that balances the benefits of edge hardening while minimizing the formation of large defects and sub-grains could lead to improved fatigue performance.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study examines the influence of punching on residual stresses, microstructural evolution, and the resulting high-cycle fatigue (HCF) behavior of hot-rolled thick-plate HSLA steel. The main conclusions are as follows: Punching significantly alters the steel’s microstructure, leading to substantial microstructural refinement, the formation of sub-grains and defects, the introduction of tensile residual stresses, and the development of a highly work-hardened shear-affected zone around the punched hole, as well as a rough fracture zone inside the hole. Residual stress in the longitudinal direction induced by punching varies through the thickness parallel to the punching direction, reaching a maximum tensile residual stress at mid-thickness of punched specimens. The lowest tensile residual stress is measured for the flat punch, while more complex punch geometries result in higher residual stresses. At high applied stresses (around 10 5  cycles), the post-punching HCF performance is comparable to that of smooth unpunched condition and is less sensitive to the differences in surface roughness, residual stress, and microstructural changes caused by various punching methods. At low applied stresses (around 10 6  cycles), the post-punching HCF strength decreases compared to the smooth unpunched condition due to surface roughness within the fracture zone and, more importantly, tensile residual stresses induced by punching. In this regime, fatigue cracks initiate at the mid-thickness, corresponding to the location of maximum measured tensile residual stress in the longitudinal direction. However, current models for predicting post-punching HCF do not fully capture the significant impact of these residual stresses, highlighting the need for experimental measurements and model refinement to improve prediction accuracy. Microstructural refinement and the formation of defects due to strain localization during punching are additional key factors in determining the post-punching HCF performance of HSLA steels. Optimizing punching geometry and parameters to balance the advantages of hardening near the punched edge while minimizing defects and sub-grains can significantly enhance post-punching fatigue performance.
